name: Old Ossetic
confidence_why: The medieval Alanic texts carry no accent marks, and the three modern reconstructions of the older Ossetic accent disagree on its very type: Thordarson (2009) holds that Old Iranian free word stress survived and that the modern strong-vowel rule arose only after the 13th century, Kim (1999) reconstructs a Sogdian-like accent on the first strong vowel (otherwise the last syllable) already for Proto-Ossetic and rejects Thordarson's evidence, and Cheung (2002, restated in Cheung 2008 and Kambolov 2006) argues for fixed initial stress and rejects Kim's.

Wien: Verlag der Oesterreichischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. Chapter 2 'Dialects', sec. 2.6.2, pp. 15-16 (open access, austriaca.at). Conflicting reachable primary: Kim, Ronald. 1999. The Origin of the Pre-Ossetic Oblique Case Suffix and its Implications. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 6.1, sec. 3 'Reconstructing Proto-Ossetic accentuation', pp. 6-9 (accent reconstruction and fn. 8 on p. 9) and sec. 4 item 6, p. 14 (open, Penn repository). Third position carried only: Cheung 2002: 121 ff. (initial stress), via Cheung 2008 n. 1 and Kambolov 2006: 327.

Kim 1999 sec. 3 pp. 6-9 (heading on p. 6), the accent reconstruction and fn. 8 both on article-internal p. 9 and sec. 4 item 6 'STRESS SHIFT' on p. 14. Kambolov 2006 p. 327 (page 326). catalog_quote: The flow of speech is divided into prosodic units of words which are syntactically connected; within the unit, one syllable bears the main accent [...] The first syllable is stressed if the vowel is long (strong); if the the vowel of the first syllable is short (weak), the accent falls on the second syllable. [...] This prosodic system is clearly an innovation which we are no doubt justified to ascribe to the influence of North Caucasian neighbour languages. The chronology of this innovation cannot be established with certainty but there may be some indications that it is comparatively recent. Vestiges of Old Iranian prosody, with a free stress accent at the word level, are found in cases where certain suffixes regularly engender vowel shortening (weakening), in connection with consonant gemination, or syncope in the preceding syllable. The most important of these cases I have treated in a previous study (Thordarson 1990). [...] As stated above, the narrowing of ā in front of nasals is later than the 13th century, which thus seems to be, as far as this evidence goes, the terminus post quem for the development of the modern prosodical system. [...] The unstressed vowel of the pænultima of the gerund suffix was thus still retained in the 13th century when the Yass tribes fled to the west from the Mongol hordes. We can admit, however, that the evidence of a single word in a document of this kind is not fully convincing.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File check: (+, extracted text) is chapter 2 'Dialects' of Thordarson 2009, Ossetic Grammatical Studies (OeAW, austriaca.at open access). The quoted passage is at lines 620-653, sec. 2.6.2, printed p. 15 running onto p. 16 (page-foot '16' falls between 'narrowing of a[macron] in front' and 'of nasals is later than the 13th century'): 'This prosodic system is clearly an innovation which we are no doubt justified to ascribe to the influence of North Caucasian neighbour languages. The chronology of this innovation cannot be established with certainty but there may be some indications that it is comparatively recent. / Vestiges of Old Iranian prosody, with a free stress accent at the word level…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Old Ossetic (Alanic, pre-13th-century) stage Thordarson reconstructs a free (lexically/morphologically determined) word-level stress accent inherited from Old Iranian, still visible in pretonic vowel weakening and syncope before certain (originally accented) suffixes; the modern Iron/Digor system (accent on the 1st syllable of the prosodic group if its vowel is strong, otherwise the 2nd) is a contact-induced innovation that arose after the 13th century. 1 and Kambolov 2006: 327) posits fixed initial stress for (pre-)Ossetic; Kim 1999 sec. 3 (= Kim 2003) posits a Sogdian-type rhythmic law, stress on the first strong/heavy vowel of the word, otherwise on the final syllable, preserved in Digor. No source states accent placement from the Alanic documents themselves.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said for the old stage (secondary accents within the prosodic group are mentioned only for the modern dialects, p. 15).
new_statements.exceptions: Evidence items rather than exceptions: ordinal suffix -aem/-aeimag, oblique forms of fars, first members of compounds (aerxud, aevdsaeron), plural daettae/daenttae, gerund -gae < oxytone *-aka instrumental, *graban- 'apparently with the accent on the final syllable' (p. 9), Yass 1422 docega retaining the unstressed penult of *docaka (p. 16, 'the evidence of a single word.. is not fully convincing').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of a reconstructed historical stage (Alanic / common Ossetic before the 13th c.), inferred from vowel weakening, syncope, loanword chronology and one Jassic spelling; not a description of accent in attested Old Ossetic texts, none of which is reported to mark stress. The modern system it is contrasted with is phrase(group)-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Old Ossetic = medieval Alanic, attested only in the Zelenchuk epitaph (10th-12th c., Greek letters), Tzetzes' Alanic verses (12th c.), the Alanic marginalia of a Greek liturgical manuscript (Lubotsky 2015) and the Yass/Jassic word list of 1422; none of these documents is described as recording accent placement in any source I opened. Every available statement about its word stress is a RECONSTRUCTION of the pre-13th-century (Alanic / Proto-Ossetic) prosodic stage inferred from modern Iron (iron1242) and Digor (digo1242) plus vowel-weakening/syncope facts, and the reconstructions disagree (Thordarson: free word-level stress inherited from Old Iranian; Cheung 2002: initial stress in (pre-)Ossetic; Kim 1999/2003: Sogdian-type rhythmic law, first heavy/strong vowel else final). Modern Ossetic (osse1243/iron1242/digo1242) is a separate catalog entity already checked.

sources.note: Phonology 3: vowel shortening before suffixes 'was caused by a dynamic stress on the following syllable at some earlier phase'; syncope 'indicative of a previous prosodic system of free dynamic accent.. which has been abandoned in the modern language'; Prosody 11: modern group accent (1st syllable if long vowel, else 2nd) 'can hardly be old, and are probably to be ascribed to the influence of some Caucasic.. languages.
